title: Anatomy Paper 1: Foundations and Systems
source: Adapted from the user-provided Anatomy Question Paper 1

objective.question: Among the four basic tissue types in the body, the correct grouping is:
objective.explanation: The four basic tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue. The supplied first option appears to have a transcription error, so it is corrected here.

objective.question: Axons, dendrites and a cell body are characteristic of cells located in:
objective.explanation: Neurons have a cell body, dendrites and an axon.

objective.question: Intercalated discs and pacemaker cells are characteristic of:
objective.explanation: Intercalated discs connect cardiac muscle cells, and specialised cardiac cells initiate and conduct pacemaker activity.

objective.question: The cribriform plate, crista galli and superior nasal conchae are parts of the:
objective.explanation: These structures are features of the ethmoid bone.

objective.question: The axial skeleton consists of the bones of the:
options: Limbs, pectoral girdle and pelvic girdle
objective.explanation: The axial skeleton includes the skull, vertebral column and thoracic cage.

objective.question: The boundaries between skull bones are immovable joints called:
objective.explanation: Most bones of the adult skull are joined by fibrous sutures.

objective.question: Subacromial, subcoracoid and subscapular bursae reduce friction in the:
objective.explanation: These bursae are associated with structures of the shoulder.

objective.question: The major abductor of the arm at the shoulder is the:
objective.explanation: The deltoid is the principal abductor of the arm after the initial movement is started by supraspinatus.

objective.question: The tough, fibrous outermost covering of the spinal cord is the:
objective.explanation: The dura mater is the tough outer meningeal layer.

objective.question: The arteriole wall layer that provides contractility and elasticity is the:
objective.explanation: The tunica media contains smooth muscle and elastic tissue.

objective.question: Blood vessels that supply the walls of large arteries and veins are called:
objective.explanation: Vasa vasorum supply the outer layers of the walls of large blood vessels.

objective.question: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are called:
objective.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, regardless of oxygen content.

objective.question: Lymph from the lower abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs is received by the:
objective.explanation: The cisterna chyli receives lymph from the lower body and continues superiorly as the thoracic duct.

objective.question: The body's largest collection of lymphoid tissue is in the:
objective.explanation: The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ.

objective.question: The large foramen between the pubic and ischial rami is the:
objective.explanation: The obturator foramen is bounded by the pubis and ischium.

objective.question: Abduction and adduction are movements associated primarily with the:
objective.explanation: Abduction and adduction are movements of appendicular structures, especially the limbs, relative to the body's midline.

objective.question: Which answer correctly distinguishes arteries from veins?
options: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return blood toward it
All arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins carry deoxygenated blood
Veins have thicker muscular walls than arteries
objective.explanation: Direction relative to the heart defines arteries and veins; pulmonary vessels are exceptions to the usual oxygenation pattern.

objective.question: Which of the following lists contains the four basic components of blood?
options: Leukocytes, bone, plasma and fibrin only
objective.explanation: Blood consists of plasma and the formed elements: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

objective.question: The correct sequence of systemic blood flow from the left ventricle toward the tissues is:
objective.explanation: Blood leaves through arteries, branches into arterioles, passes through capillaries, then returns through venules and veins.

objective.question: Muscles of facial expression are innervated by cranial nerve:
objective.explanation: The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) supplies the muscles of facial expression.

objective.question: The strongest muscle of mastication is generally considered the:
objective.explanation: The masseter is a powerful jaw-closing muscle and is commonly described as the strongest muscle of mastication.

objective.question: Another term for a muscle cell is:
objective.explanation: A skeletal muscle cell is commonly called a muscle fibre.

objective.question: Which muscle types contain sarcomeres?
objective.explanation: Sarcomeres are the contractile units of striated skeletal and cardiac muscle; smooth muscle does not have sarcomeres.

structured.question: List the four axial muscles of mastication.
markingGuide: Masseter: 2 marks.
Temporalis: 2 marks.
Medial pterygoid: 2 marks.
Lateral pterygoid: 2 marks.
Award remaining 2 marks for correctly identifying all four as muscles of mastication and clear naming.
structured.modelAnswer: The four muscles of mastication are masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid.

structured.question: Name the four spinal curvatures present in an adult and state their directions.
markingGuide: Cervical curvature: lordotic, convex anteriorly: 2 marks.
Thoracic curvature: kyphotic, convex posteriorly: 2 marks.
Lumbar curvature: lordotic, convex anteriorly: 2 marks.
Sacral curvature: kyphotic, convex posteriorly: 2 marks.
Correctly distinguishes primary and secondary curves: 2 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: The adult vertebral column has cervical and lumbar lordoses (convex anteriorly) and thoracic and sacral kyphoses (convex posteriorly). Thoracic and sacral curves are primary; cervical and lumbar curves develop after birth.

structured.question: List the four bones in the proximal row of the carpus, from lateral to medial in anatomical position.
markingGuide: Scaphoid: 2 marks.
Lunate: 2 marks.
Triquetrum: 2 marks.
Pisiform: 2 marks.
Correct lateral-to-medial order: 2 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: From lateral (thumb side) to medial, the proximal carpal row is scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform.

structured.question: Name the three regions of the oesophagus.
markingGuide: Cervical part: 3 marks.
Thoracic part: 3 marks.
Abdominal part: 3 marks.
Identifies their order from superior to inferior: 1 mark.
structured.modelAnswer: The oesophagus has cervical, thoracic and short abdominal parts, in that order.

structured.question: State five functions of the skin.
markingGuide: Any five valid functions, 2 marks each: protection/barrier; thermoregulation; cutaneous sensation; vitamin D synthesis; prevention of water loss; immune defence; excretion of small amounts of sweat; blood reservoir.
structured.modelAnswer: Functions include protecting against mechanical, chemical and microbial injury; reducing water loss; regulating temperature through sweating and blood flow; providing sensation; synthesising vitamin D; contributing to immune defence; and excreting small amounts of water, salts and urea in sweat.

structured.question: (a) Explain the nerve supply to the extraocular muscles. (b) Name the seven tarsal bones. (c) List the three meninges of the brain. (d) Name four motor cranial nerves.
markingGuide: (a) CN III supplies superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris: 5 marks.
(a) CN IV supplies superior oblique: 2 marks.
(a) CN VI supplies lateral rectus: 2 marks.
(b) Names talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms: 4 marks.
(c) Names dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater: 3 marks.
(d) Gives four motor nerves, e.g. III, IV, VI, XI or XII: 4 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: The extraocular muscles are supplied by cranial nerve III except superior oblique (CN IV) and lateral rectus (CN VI). The seven tarsals are talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms. The meninges are dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. Four predominantly motor cranial nerves include III, IV, VI, XI and XII (any four).

structured.question: (a) List five major foramina of the skull and one structure passing through each. (b) Describe the blood supply to the brain.
markingGuide: Five correct skull foramina with an associated structure, 2 marks each: 10 marks.
Identifies internal carotid and vertebral arteries as the main arterial sources: 2 marks.
Describes vertebral arteries joining as basilar artery and contributing posterior cerebral arteries: 3 marks.
Describes internal carotid contributions to anterior and middle cerebral arteries: 3 marks.
Explains anterior and posterior communicating arteries and the Circle of Willis: 2 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: Examples include foramen magnum—medulla/spinal cord and vertebral arteries; optic canal—optic nerve and ophthalmic artery; superior orbital fissure—CN III, IV, V1 and VI; foramen ovale—CN V3; jugular foramen—CN IX, X and XI. The paired vertebral arteries enter the skull through the foramen magnum and join to form the basilar artery, which contributes to the posterior cerebral arteries. Each internal carotid artery gives rise to anterior and middle cerebral arteries. Anterior communicating and posterior communicating arteries connect these vessels to form the Circle of Willis, providing collateral pathways at the brain's base.

structured.question: (a) Describe and label the main parts of the scapula. (b) List four parts of the digestive system. (c) Name six muscles of facial expression.
markingGuide: (a) Identifies spine, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity, borders/angles and major fossae: 10 marks.
(b) Gives four valid digestive tract or accessory-organ components: 4 marks.
(c) Gives six correct facial-expression muscles: 6 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: The scapula has a spine dividing posterior supraspinous and infraspinous fossae, a subscapular fossa on its anterior surface, an acromion and coracoid process, a lateral glenoid cavity, three borders (superior, medial and lateral), and three angles (superior, inferior and lateral). Digestive-system parts include the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, pancreas and gallbladder. Facial-expression muscles include orbicularis oculi, orbicularis oris, buccinator, zygomaticus major, zygomaticus minor, frontalis, platysma and risorius (any six).
